text: Threat modeling tells you how to find risks specific to your own system. The OWASP Top 10 is the industry's shared vocabulary for the risk categories that show up again and again, across almost every web application — including the services Northbridge Retail runs. You don't need to memorize all ten, but you do need to recognize them by name, because they're what your scanning tools in Chapter 4 will report back to you.

OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, is a nonprofit that publishes free, community-driven application security resources. The Top 10 is its best-known project: a ranked list of the most critical web risk categories, rebuilt periodically from real-world vulnerability data. It isn't ten specific bugs — each entry is a category covering a family of related weaknesses. The current ten: Broken Access Control, Security Misconfiguration, Software Supply Chain Failures, Cryptographic Failures, Injection, Insecure Design, Authentication Failures, Software or Data Integrity Failures, Security Logging and Alerting Failures, and Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.

As a platform engineer at Northbridge Retail, you're less likely to personally write an injection bug, and far more likely to configure the pipeline that catches it. Three categories sit closest to your daily tooling decisions: Security Misconfiguration, your infrastructure-as-code and container defaults; Software Supply Chain Failures, your dependency and build-pipeline integrity, the direct subject of Chapters 4 and 5; and Security Logging and Alerting Failures, your observability and audit trail, covered in Chapter 6.

The list is a prioritization aid, not a ceiling — it represents the most commonly found categories, not an exhaustive catalog of every risk Northbridge's systems could face. A good scanning and threat-modeling practice will surface plenty of findings that don't map neatly to any Top 10 entry, and that's expected. Next up, Lesson 4: where security fits across the whole software lifecycle.
